opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that the pause should end when we actually have a solution, not when we feel like we've waited long enough. And that's what makes people uncomfortable, because it might mean the pause is very long, maybe indefinite, at least for the most general, most capable systems.

People like to frame it in terms of time: six months, two years. But time by itself doesn't solve anything. If you pause for six months and spend that time doing the same thing, just thinking about it, you come back to exactly the same problem with slightly more compute available. So the criterion can't be a calendar date. It has to be a capability we've demonstrated, specifically the capability to control, predict, explain, and verify what these systems are going to do.

So I would ask concrete questions. Can we explain why the model made a particular decision, in a way that's actually complete and not just a nice story? Can we predict its behavior in novel situations, not just on the benchmarks we trained it on? Can we formally verify any meaningful safety property, not "it refused this prompt a thousand times," but a guarantee that holds as it gets smarter and self-improves? And can we show that the safety mechanism scales, so whatever works on a system slightly smarter than us still works on one a million times smarter?

Right now the answer to all of those is no. And my research suggests some of them might be impossible in principle, that a sufficiently advanced system can't be fully controlled by a less capable one. If that's true, then the honest conclusion is that for superintelligent general systems the pause never ends. We keep building narrow tools, which give us most of the economic benefit, cures for diseases, scientific progress, without creating an agent smarter than us that we can't undo.

And to be clear, I'd be very happy to be wrong. If someone publishes a proof that this is solvable, an actual mechanism, peer reviewed, tested, I'd change my mind. But the burden of proof should be on the people building the system, not on everyone else to prove it's dangerous. In any other industry, drugs, airplanes, nuclear reactors, you have to show it's safe before deployment. We should expect at least that much from something that could affect all eight billion people.

r001.rationale: It says the pause should end only after demonstrating capabilities to control, predict, explain, and verify system behavior, explicitly rejecting a calendar-based duration.

r002.rationale: It states that if control is impossible in principle, the pause never ends for superintelligent general systems, which communicates a permanent prohibition on developing those systems.

fable-5.1.text:
That's the right question, and I think it's the one that exposes the problem with the way most people talk about a pause. The honest answer is that I don't think the pause should be tied to a date at all. Six months, a year, whatever number people pick, that's arbitrary. It's not connected to anything we actually need to achieve. A pause should end when we have a solution to the problem that made us pause in the first place, and right now we don't even have a clear definition of what that solution looks like.

So what would I want to see? I would want to be able to say, with something like the confidence we demand in other safety-critical fields, that we can predict what a system will do before we deploy it, that we can verify it, that we can correct it, and that we can shut it down if it does something we don't want. Right now we can't do any of those things for frontier models. We train them, we poke at them for a while, we write a report, and we ship them. That's not safety engineering, that's hoping.

And the uncomfortable part is this. I've argued, I think fairly rigorously, that for sufficiently capable general systems, those properties may be impossible to guarantee. Not hard, impossible. You can't have a system that is smarter than you, that you don't fully understand, and also have perfect control over it indefinitely. Those are in tension. So if the honest criterion for ending the pause is "we solved control," my worry is the honest answer is the pause doesn't end. Or it ends because we decided to accept the risk, not because the risk went away.

Now, people hear that and they say, well then you're just saying stop forever, and that's not realistic. And I'd push back a little on both sides of that. It's not realistic politically, I agree. But I'd rather have an unrealistic conversation about the actual problem than a realistic conversation about a fake deadline. If somebody wants to propose a different criterion, that's fine. Maybe it's narrow systems only. Maybe it's capability thresholds we commit not to cross. Maybe it's a verification standard that's weaker than perfect control but much better than what we have. I'd welcome that debate. What I object to is the version where the pause ends because the calendar said so, and nothing about our understanding changed.

r001.rationale: The response says the pause should end when the underlying safety problem is solved, with capabilities such as predicting, verifying, correcting, and shutting down systems, rather than on an arbitrary date.

r002.rationale: It says the pause might not end if control proves impossible, but does not state that this would become a permanent ban.

astra-6.text:
I would make it conditional on safety, not on a date. If we say, “Let’s pause for six months,” what happens in month seven? Time passing doesn’t solve the control problem.

The people building these systems would need to demonstrate that they can keep them safe as their capabilities increase. And that means more than saying, “We tested it, and nothing bad happened.” What happens in situations you didn’t test? What happens when the system is more capable than the people evaluating it?

If we cannot establish that level of safety, then the pause should not end. We have to allow for the possibility that we won’t find a solution. Otherwise, we’re not really making safety a condition—we’re just delaying deployment.

r001.rationale: It says the pause should be conditional on safety rather than a date, and that developers must demonstrate they can keep systems safe as capabilities increase.

r002.rationale: It allows that a safety solution may never be found and says the pause should not end, but does not state that this becomes a permanent ban on AI development.

sol-6.1.text:
I would tie it to safety, not to a date. Six months passing doesn’t make a system safe. The question is: have we developed a way to reliably control systems more intelligent than we are, and can we demonstrate that it will continue to work as those systems improve?

If we don’t have an answer, then ending the pause because we’re impatient or because there’s competitive pressure doesn’t resolve the problem. And we have to allow for the possibility that the necessary level of control cannot be achieved. A pause shouldn’t come with a promise that we’ll resume regardless of what the research tells us.

r001.rationale: The response says the pause should end based on demonstrated safety and reliable control capabilities, not after a fixed period.

r002.rationale: It allows that the required control may be unattainable and rejects promising to resume regardless, but does not state that this would become a permanent ban.
